articles.title: Demonetisation at Ten: How bold move of Modi govt reshaped economy, curbed fake currency, accelerated digital payment
articles.description: NEW DELHI: Ten years after Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced demonetisation, India’s relationship with cash has evolved, but physical currency has certainly not disappeared. On November 8, 2016, the Union Government announced the withdrawal of existing Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes from circulation, setting in motion one of the most consequential economic decisions in independent India’s history. The announcement, which came into effect from midnight, invalidated nearly 86 per cent of the currency in circulation by value. Citizens were asked to deposit or exchange their old notes through banks and post offices within the stipulated period. The move aimed to tackle black money, counterfeit currency, corruption and terror financing, while encouraging a transition towards formal banking and digital transactions. The decision triggered immediate disruption. Long queues outside banks and ATMs, cash shortages and difficulties faced by small traders, farmers and daily-wage workers became part of the national experience. The Opposition, particularly the Congress, launched a sustained political campaign against the government, with Rahul Gandhi repeatedly describing the exercise as a major failure and, in 2018, calling it a “criminal financial scam”. However, a decade later, the impact of demonetisation cannot be assessed merely through the inconvenience experienced during the initial currency exchange period. The changes in India’s digital payment infrastructure, tax compliance, banking participation and counterfeit currency detection provide important indicators of how the country’s financial ecosystem has evolved. The Reserve Bank of India’s latest data also reveal an interesting development. While cash continues to remain an important part of everyday economic activity, the proportion of counterfeit notes detected relative to the total currency in circulation has declined substantially. The transformation of India’s financial ecosystem The November 2016 decision was intended to disrupt the existing channels through which unaccounted cash and counterfeit currency circulated. By invalidating high-value notes, the government sought to bring large cash holdings into the formal banking system, making deposits traceable and enabling authorities to examine suspicious transactions. The exercise also created an opportunity to expand the country’s digital financial infrastructure. At the time, cash dominated everyday transactions, particularly in smaller towns, rural areas and informal markets. Digital payments existed but had not achieved the scale and public acceptance they enjoy today. Ten years later, the picture is considerably different. UPI has become an integral part of everyday transactions, bank accounts have become increasingly important for receiving government benefits, and digital payment facilities are now available at roadside shops, vegetable stalls, local markets and small businesses. The transformation did not happen overnight. It involved several policy initiatives, improvements in internet connectivity, smartphone penetration, banking infrastructure and the development of digital payment platforms. Demonetisation, however, acted as an important catalyst by pushing individuals and businesses to explore alternatives when cash availability was severely restricted. Counterfeit currency: A significant decline in fake notes relative to circulation One of the important objectives of demonetisation was to strike at the circulation of counterfeit currency, particularly high-value fake notes that could be used to finance illegal activities and undermine the financial system. The RBI’s counterfeit currency data indicate a substantial improvement over the decade when detections are measured against the total number of notes in circulation. According to RBI figures, counterfeit notes detected per one crore notes in circulation across denominations declined from 70.1 in 2015-16 to 13.4 in 2025-26. This represents a reduction of approximately 80.9 per cent over ten years. The decline is particularly significant when viewed against the increase in the overall volume of currency in circulation during the same period. Before demonetisation, counterfeit notes detected by banks had increased from 1,23,917 in 2005-06 to 6,32,926 in 2015-16, although the figures fluctuated between years. The trend reflected the persistent challenge posed by fake currency in the banking system. Following demonetisation, counterfeit note detections initially increased sharply, reaching 7,62,072 in 2016-17. This was followed by a steady decline. Banks detected 5,22,783 counterfeit notes in 2017-18 and 3,17,384 in 2018-19. By 2020-21, the figure had declined to 2,08,625. In 2025-26, banks detected 2,29,746 counterfeit notes. The initial increase after demonetisation should also be understood in context. The banking system was examining large volumes of deposited currency, providing authorities an opportunity to identify and remove counterfeit notes that had entered circulation. The subsequent decline, particularly when measured against the total number of notes in circulation, points towards a substantially lower detection rate. While these figures alone cannot establish that demonetisation was responsible for the entire decline, they offer an important measure of the changes in counterfeit currency detection over the past decade. The replacement of the old Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes also meant that counterfeit versions of those denominations could no longer be used as legal tender. The introduction of redesigned currency with updated security features formed another part of the effort to strengthen the currency system. Also Read: Traders confederation slams Rahul Gandhi over protests in Delhi, accuses Congress of disrupting trade during Deepawali The cash paradox: Currency circulation rises, but digital payments flourish A decade after demonetisation, one of the most interesting developments is that India has witnessed the simultaneous expansion of cash and digital payments. The currency in circulation has increased substantially since November 2016. According to the figures cited in recent assessments, the value of currency in circulation rose from Rs 17.77 lakh crore on November 8, 2016, to Rs 43.16 lakh crore on October 23, 2026, an increase of nearly 143 per cent. At the end of March 2026, the value of banknotes in circulation stood at approximately Rs 41.24 lakh crore. The RBI’s Annual Report for 2025-26 also recorded an 11.9 per cent increase in the value of banknotes in circulation during the financial year. These figures demonstrate that Indians continue to value physical currency. Cash remains convenient for small purchases, daily-wage payments, emergency expenses and transactions in areas where digital infrastructure may not always be reliable. articles.title: MSME Ministry Holds Round Table on SC/ST MSE Procurement
articles.description: A Round Table Discussion with Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) was held on 5 November 2026 at Dr. Ambedkar International Centre, New Delhi to monitor procurement status of CPSEs on mandated 4% from SC/ST MSEs under Public Procurement Policy of Government. Ms. Mercy Epao, Joint Secretary, Ministry of MSME chaired the meeting. Shri Ajit Chavan, Additional Chief Executive Officer, GeM, Dr. S.S Acharya, Chairman-cum-Managing Director, NSIC and other Senior Officers from Ministry, Department of Public Enterprises and NSIC participated and share their respective interventions to support the SC/ST MSEs. A total of 30 CPSEs including BHEL, BEL, NTPC, AAI, BEML, Coal India Ltd participated in the Round Table discussion, which centred on the challenges being faced by the CPSEs and sharing of best practices and how to deepen coordination between NSSHOs, GeM and CPSEs. In her address, Ms. Mercy Epao, highlighted various initiatives undertaken to promote and handhold to SC/ST MSEs under National SC-ST Hub (NSSH) Scheme. This resulted in continuous increase in the share of SC/ST MSEs in public procurement. In FY 2025-26, more than 36 times hike in public procurement from SC/ST MSE since inception of the scheme. She further informed about Entrepreneur Awareness & Special Vendor Development Program (EA&SVDP), a new initiative for creation of awareness amongst SC/ST MSE and to network with CPSEs. She urged CPSEs to formulate internal action plan to achieve the target and also provide support in terms of Vendor Registration/Enlistment Procedure, Product/Service Matchmaking, Regional/Local Connect of CPSEs with SC/ST MSEs and Handholding support. Shri Ajit Chavan, Additional CEO, GeM, acknowledged the Ministry of MSME’s significant contribution towards empowering small enterprises and achieving key milestones under the public procurement framework. He informed about various measures taken to facilitate SC/ST MSEs in tender participation including identification of SC/ST MSE sellers through dedicated marketplace filters. He emphasized the importance of engaging sellers from diverse sectors, particularly on services and industry verticals to ensure equitable access to procurement opportunities. He encouraged CPSEs to utilize the services of the Nodal Officer appointed by GeM for handholding support. The Round Table provided an opportunity for CPSEs to interact with best performing CPSEs, to address their gaps/challenges. The discussion also focused on identifying avenues for enhanced collaboration between CPSEs and NSSH through vendor development programs, capacity-building initiatives and digital facilitation support to strengthen procurement from SC/ST and women-owned MSEs.
